title: Data Centers Are Driving an Alarming Gas Power Expansion in the US
gist: Global Energy Monitor's mid-2026 update finds the US pipeline of gas-fired power being developed exclusively for data centers has jumped to more than 189 gigawatts, roughly doubling from 97 GW at end-2025 and up from just 4 GW in early 2024. The data-center boom has pushed the US back past China in gas projects in the pipeline, even as China's own data-center buildout leans on solar and hydropower.

insights.claim: US gas-fired power capacity in development exclusively for data centers has risen to more than 189 gigawatts as of mid-2026, up from 97 GW at the end of 2025 and 4 GW in early 2024, according to Global Energy Monitor tracking.
insights.so_what: A ~47x rise in two years is the demand signal for gas turbines, pipeline capacity, and EPC contractors; size positions against the tracked pipeline, not against announced AI capex alone.
insights.quote: In January, the group found that there were 97 gigawatts of gas projects in development exclusively for data centers at the end of 2025, a massive increase from just 4 gigawatts tracked in early 2024.

insights.speaker: Molly Taft

insights.claim: A gigawatt of power capacity is roughly equivalent to the electricity needed for a million homes, making the 189 GW data-center gas pipeline comparable in scale to powering 189 million households.
insights.so_what: Useful unit conversion for sanity-checking any AI-power headline against residential load and ratepayer politics.
insights.quote: (A gigawatt can power roughly a million homes.)
insights.locator: Now, in an update to the research released Tuesday
insights.speaker: Molly Taft

insights.claim: Gas power buildout in the US can no longer be analyzed independently of the data-center buildout, because the two pipelines are now directly coupled.
insights.so_what: Treat US gas demand forecasts as a derivative of AI capex forecasts; a slowdown in one transmits directly to the other.
insights.quote: “Increasingly, the US gas power buildout is getting tied directly to the data center buildout—you can’t talk about one without the other,”
insights.speaker: Molly Taft

insights.claim: Data center builders are increasingly using private 'behind-the-meter' power plants specifically to bypass lengthy grid interconnection queues, turning generation from a utility service into an in-house build decision.
insights.so_what: Value migrates to turbine suppliers and private developers rather than regulated utilities; interconnection-queue reform matters less to AI timelines than it used to.
insights.quote: data center builders have increasingly turned to private power facilities, known as behind-the-meter plants, to bypass lengthy grid connection times

insights.speaker: Molly Taft

insights.claim: Behind-the-meter generation is being framed as a way to avoid pushing data-center costs onto utility ratepayers, an issue that has become a political flashpoint as local opposition to data centers mounts.
insights.so_what: Ratepayer backlash is the key regulatory risk to watch for grid-connected data-center projects; private power is the industry's political hedge.
insights.quote: This approach can also potentially help avoid saddling ratepayers with higher bills, an issue that’s become a flashpoint as data center opposition mounts around the country.

insights.claim: The Trump administration has introduced a voluntary pledge encouraging tech companies to bring their own power, signed by Microsoft, Meta, Google and OpenAI along with Republican governors and major utilities.
insights.so_what: Federal policy is actively subsidizing the private-gas path; expect permitting tailwinds for behind-the-meter gas over grid-scale renewables in the US.
insights.quote: The Trump administration has encouraged tech companies to bring their own power, introducing a voluntary pledge that’s been signed by the likes of Microsoft, Meta, Google, and OpenAI
insights.locator: The Trump administration has encouraged tech companies
insights.speaker: Molly Taft

insights.claim: Many of the new data-center gas facilities are being built with inefficient turbines, which raises emissions per unit of power beyond what a modern gas fleet would produce.
insights.so_what: Emissions intensity of AI compute is worse than headline gas-vs-coal math implies; a live input for any ESG or carbon-liability screen on hyperscalers.
insights.quote: particularly because many of the facilities are being built with inefficient turbines, which can increase emissions
insights.locator: Adding that much natural gas power comes with a hefty climate cost
insights.speaker: Molly Taft

insights.claim: Some individual data-center gas plants are permitted to emit more greenhouse gases per year than many small- and medium-sized countries.
insights.so_what: Single-asset emissions of this scale invite targeted litigation and state-level permitting fights; site-level permits are the disclosure to read.
insights.quote: some of these gas plants are permitted to emit more greenhouse gases each year than many small- and medium-sized countries

insights.claim: Not all tracked gas projects will be built — financing, local opposition, moratoriums and turbine supply constraints all sit between announcement and construction — but any that are built lock in emissions for decades.
insights.so_what: Discount the 189 GW headline for attrition, but treat turbine supply constraints as the binding physical bottleneck worth tracking on the supply side.
insights.quote: “There's a lot of uncertainty: financing, your local opposition, data, your moratoriums, the turbine constraints to supply equipment—there's so many factors,”

themes.theme: US vs China energy strategy divergence

insights.claim: The data-center boom has pushed the US back past China as the country with the most gas projects in the pipeline, reversing the early-2020s period when China outpaced US gas plant construction.
insights.so_what: US LNG and domestic gas demand gets a structural bid from AI, while China's marginal gas demand stays tied to fertilizer and plastics rather than compute.
insights.quote: The data center boom means that the US has again surpassed China as the country with the most gas projects in the pipeline, according to Global Energy Monitor.
insights.locator: But the country does have a modest fleet of natural gas plants
insights.speaker: Molly Taft

insights.claim: China's data-center buildout is oriented around renewables — especially solar and hydropower — with facilities sited in rural areas that have excess renewable production, and only smaller attempts at private power.
insights.so_what: Undercuts the 'China needs fossil fuels to win the AI race' framing; Chinese solar and hydro supply chains capture the compute-power spend that gas captures in the US.
insights.quote: “Overall, the data center boom in China is really oriented around renewables,”
insights.locator: “Overall, the data center boom in China
insights.speaker: Molly Taft

insights.claim: China's grid-side renewables buildout is described as a deliberate government choice aimed at energy independence, not merely a cost-driven outcome.
insights.so_what: Policy-driven demand is less price-elastic; Chinese renewable capex is unlikely to fall with commodity cycles.
insights.locator: He adds that the Chinese buildout of renewables on the grid
insights.speaker: Molly Taft

insights.claim: Building gas for US data centers may make near-term economic sense given the absence of cheap renewable energy at Chinese scale, but the long-term price is paid in emissions and in underinvestment in the domestic clean energy sector.
insights.so_what: The trade is long US gas near-term, but watch for a policy snapback that repricing US clean-energy manufacturers on competitiveness grounds.
insights.quote: “But over the long term, you pay a price for that—obviously, in terms of emissions, but also, I think in terms of not investing in your own clean energy sector.”
